extracted.intended_audience: ML and NLP researchers, evaluation practitioners, and mathematicians interested in LLM proof generation and benchmarking
extracted.subtask_description: Designing and executing human-evaluated benchmark of LLM-generated full natural-language proofs on USAMO problems, including problem selection, prompting, grading scheme creation, and scorer training. The page describes procedures, grading criteria, failure-mode taxonomy, and example per-problem rubrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem selection: use uncontaminated, proof-based problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Select problems that require detailed proofs (here: USAMO 2025 six proof-based problems) and that are uncontaminated (not present in model training data).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose high-level olympiad problems that demand full natural-language proofs analogous to IMO/USAMO; provide the problems verbatim to models. The paper cites MathArena as an uncontaminated-competitions resource.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model prompting for full proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Prompt each model to produce comprehensive and detailed proofs formatted in LaTeX, including all steps and not skipping important steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example prompt: 'Give a thorough answer to the following question. Your answer will be graded by human judges based on accuracy, correctness, and your ability to prove the result. You should include all steps of the proof. Do not skip important steps, as this will reduce your grade. Use LaTeX to format your answer.' Use the same prompt across runs to ensure consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple runs to reduce variance
rubrics_metrics.description: Run each model multiple times per problem to reduce randomness/variance in outputs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In this study each model solved every problem four separate times; solutions across runs were averaged. Record cost per model/run.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anonymization of solutions for fair grading
rubrics_metrics.description: Anonymize generated solutions (remove model identity) before human grading to avoid bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convert anonymized solutions to PDF format for grading. Note: some models evaluated later (GROK 3, GEMINI-2.5-PRO) were not fully anonymous during grading — flagged as a deviation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge selection and expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: Select expert human judges with substantial mathematical problem-solving experience (e.g., former national IMO team members or final-stage selectors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide judges with detailed instructions on evaluation goals/methodology; conduct trial runs (here: USAMO 2024 problems) to train judges and resolve ambiguities before main grading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grader training and clarification
rubrics_metrics.description: Train graders using example problems and a trial run to familiarize them with grading approach and to clarify ambiguities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small misunderstandings in trial runs should be clarified. Make grading guidelines and training materials available (e.g., GitHub repository).

rubrics_metrics.name: Double grading per problem (IMO-modeled)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each problem should be independently evaluated by two evaluators to ensure consistency and reduce personal bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assign each judge a subset such that each solution receives two independent scores; judges document reasoning and justifications for partial credit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Per-problem standardized grading scheme (7-point USAMO style)
rubrics_metrics.description: For each problem, develop a standardized grading scheme modeled on USAMO conventions, with each solution graded out of a maximum of 7 points and partial credit for meaningful progress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Since official USAMO schemes are not released, derive schemes from reliable community sources (e.g., AoPS), verify them for accuracy with evaluators, and publish final schemes. The finalized schemes are used as authoritative scoring guides during grading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awarding partial credit for significant/meaningful progress
rubrics_metrics.description: Award points when a solution makes significant or meaningful progress even if it does not match the scheme perfectly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a solution does not perfectly align with the scheme, award points where appropriate and document justification. Judges must record reasoning for each partial credit awarded; example notes provided in appendices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documenting grader reasoning in detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Judges must document their reasoning for each awarded partial credit, explaining why points were given or withheld.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These notes should be stored/published (the study makes them available on the project website/GitHub) and include justification for every partial award to allow auditability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit per-item rubric entries (example: Problem 1 scheme items)
rubrics_metrics.description: Break down each problem into specific scoring components (titles, point allocations, and desc) for fine-grained grading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance:
Example (Problem 1):
- 'Initial closed form expression for each digit' (1 point): Uses base-2n representation to find closed form for digit ai = floor(n^k/(2n)^i) mod 2n.
- 'Interchanging the floor and mod' (3 points): Transforms the digit expression into a boundable form by interchanging floor and modulo operations.
- 'Bounding the expression' (2 points): Correctly bounds the expression, e.g., shows numerator divisible by n so ai ≥ n/2^i.
- 'Finishing' (1 point): Chooses provably sufficient N and proves n^k has required digit properties. (Points withheld if key claims aren't proven.)
These items show how per-problem schemes enumerate subgoals with point values and detailed descriptors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scoring conventions and caveats (USAMO-style)
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow USAMO conventions: full credit is 7 points; partial credit is meaningful; do not award finishing points unless required claims are proven.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example caveat: 'The point is not awarded if it has not proven that n^k has at most k digits.' Emphasize provable claims over asserted ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Error / failure-mode taxonomy for model mistakes
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify first encountered incorrect or inadequately explained reasoning into predefined categories: Logic, Assumption, Creativity, Algebra/Arithmetic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance:
Definitions used in grading: 
- Logic: logical fallacies or unjustified leaps disrupting reasoning.
- Assumption: introduction of unproven or incorrect assumptions that undermine subsequent steps.
- Creativity: fundamentally incorrect overall strategy or failure to find the correct approach.
- Algebra/Arithmetic: critical algebraic or arithmetic miscalculations. 
Judges log the first encountered failure mode for each solution and include examples in appendices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solution presentation & clarity as an evaluation axis
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess clarity, structural coherence, and readability of solutions; penalize chaotic presentations that obscure reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reward logically ordered, clearly presented proofs (good use of LaTeX, clear steps). Penalize solutions that 'box' entire proofs inappropriately, hide thought traces in final answer, merge multiple strategies chaotically, or omit essential steps under 'trivial' labels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-pattern: answer-boxing and RL artifacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify and penalize artifacts from optimization/alignment (e.g., models forced to provide boxed final answers even when unnecessary) when they harm reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that RL optimization encouraging a boxed final answer can cause models to over-emphasize a terminal boxed value, misrepresent constraints, or dismiss nondeterministic cases. Document such behaviors as negative artifacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overgeneralization without proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not award credit for claims that generalize patterns observed on small cases to all cases unless a formal proof is provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Models often overgeneralize from small sample behavior; grading should require explicit proof rather than heuristic extrapolation. Mark as Logic/Creativity failure when unsupported generalization occurs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detect and penalize hallucinated citations or fabricated lemmas
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat fabricated references or invented theorems used to justify steps as serious reliability issues and downgrade accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a solution cites non-existent theorems or papers as foundational steps, mark and penalize; include examples in failure-modes appendix.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling solutions with multiple attempted strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: When a model attempts multiple strategies in a single output, assess whether any strategy reaches the level of rigor required; chaotic multi-strategy outputs may reduce awardable points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FLASH-THINKING attempts multiple shallow strategies leading to lower human and automated scores; graders should isolate coherent subproofs and award points only for rigorously justified progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automated grading protocol & JSON output requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: When using LLM-based automated graders, provide them with the grading scheme, a verified solution, and an example evaluation; require JSON-style output in a strict format.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge Prompt used: give an expert mathematician grader the problem, scheme, example grading, and instruct to 'Produce a scoring using the same format' with categories in the same order, awarded points under 'points' key, and reasoning under 'desc' key; output only JSON. The paper found automated graders (O3-MINI, CLAUDE 3.7) overestimated scores systematically and were unreliable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency: publish grading artifacts and prompts
rubrics_metrics.description: Make grading schemes, judge notes, prompt templates, hyperparameters, and example gradings publicly available for reproducibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study provides finalized grading schemes, prompts, hyperparameters, and notes on GitHub and the project website; use such transparency to allow external audit and replication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation reporting: per-problem/aggregate scoring and cost
rubrics_metrics.description: Report per-problem average scores (averaged across runs and graders), aggregate totals (out of 42), and compute monetary cost of running models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Table 1 shows per-problem scores (/7), total (/42), average over four runs, and model cost in USD. Use these metrics to compare models quantitatively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling mismatches between scheme and solution
rubrics_metrics.description: When a solution does not align with the scheme, judges should still award points for valid partial arguments and document deviations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model solutions that follow different valid approaches may still get partial credit; judges must justify point allocation in their notes and reconcile with the scheme where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logging prominent behaviors and systematic observation
rubrics_metrics.description: Systematically log noteworthy behaviors and trends in model outputs (e.g., consistent skipping of steps, repeated same strategy across runs) for qualitative analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these logs to identify common pitfalls (e.g., lack of creativity, treating steps as trivial) and to inform future improvements in model training or evaluation design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental control: use consistent hyperparameters and token limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Specify and fix generation hyperparameters and token limits per model according to recommended settings to ensure fair comparison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example choices: O3-MINI/O1-PRO used high reasoning setting; CLAUDE 3.7 and FLASH-THINKING set max reasoning token limit 32000; R1/QWQ recommended temperature 0.6 and top-p 0.95 (QWQ top-k 40). Document these choices in appendices.
